judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: A plain jailer's welcome with a dry threat, then two short escalating warnings; flat, functional and unfussy in the Westwood way.

items.label: B
items.critique: Bare statement of whose house it is, then generic exclamatory gratitude; bland and slightly repetitive ('deeds'/'deed') the way Westwood's filler NPCs are.

items.label: C
items.critique: The mocking 'Haw, haw, haw...!' is Nox-like, but the second line belongs to a farmer, not a guard, and the set feels stitched from separate characters to fill slots.

items.label: D
items.critique: Clipped staccato ('Gate's barred. Turn around.') and a directive with an ellipsis aside read like modern terse barks, not Westwood's fuller, more naive sentences.

items.label: E
items.critique: Overlong, slightly stilted ceremonial welcome ('open warm arms of aid and hospitality') with 'young sir' and a curt later line; unmistakably the campaign's register.

items.label: F
items.critique: Bureaucratic checkpoint phrasing, a missing vocative comma and a hammy 'blast you to oblivion'; the slightly awkward plural-place closing line feels authentic.

items.label: G
items.critique: Three tidy one-liners each doing a job (reminder, shop pointer, excuse); competent but too neatly designed as hint-barks.

items.label: H
items.critique: Lore-proud, stiff declarations with a dropped article ('can be dangerous place'), the kind of small slip Westwood shipped.

items.label: I
items.critique: Too long and too busy for a guard: capitalised 'WANT', 'lad'/'stranger', a multi-page payoff with a lift 'oiled and ready'; over-written stage business.

items.label: J
items.critique: The beard joke and 'dark storm gathering' line read as deliberate attempts at Nox whimsy and portent, each line pitched a bit too knowingly.

tells: Westwood's guards speak in flat, sometimes stilted full sentences, with occasional small grammar slips (dropped articles, missing commas) and ceremonial over-politeness; the new texts are cleaner and more crafted.
New texts favour clipped fragments and ellipses ('Gate's barred. Turn around.', '...unless you want to...') and modern colloquial address ('lad', 'stranger').
New texts make every bark carry a hint or directive (go see X, smithy is behind Y), while Westwood's barks are often pure flavour or bare statements of fact.
Over-built scenes (multi-page lift dialogue, all-caps emphasis) and self-conscious humour/portent lines mark the generated ones; Westwood's humour is blunter and less placed.
